section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department despatches, internal memoranda, military intelligence reports, diplomatic telegrams, cross-reference sheets, and press clippings concerning proceedings of the 67th and 68th Japanese Imperial Diet sessions and related foreign policy issues between January 1935 and February 1936. Major foreign affairs topics include Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's Diet addresses on naval disarmament, the termination of the Washington Naval Treaty, and relations with the Soviet Union and China, accompanied by diplomatic commentary from Moscow, Shanghai, and Nanking. Domestic coverage centers on political maneuvering by the Seiyukai opposition against the non-party Okada Cabinet, parliamentary debates regarding military spending, attacks on Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's Emperor-organ constitutional theory, the obstruction of agricultural relief and economic control bills, and the eventual dissolution of the Diet in January 1936.

subfiles.about: Newspaper clipping reporting the text of Japanese Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's foreign policy address delivered before the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Hirota's Diet address: London naval talks, termination of the Washington Naval Treaty, North Manchuria Railway negotiations with the USSR, Chinese Communist movements, and a call for solidarity before League withdrawal.
subfiles.title: Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's Address on Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Despatch from the American Embassy in Moscow reporting on Soviet press and official reactions to Foreign Minister Hirota's Diet address.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires John C. Wiley reports that Foreign Minister Hirota's speech was received with generally conciliatory comments in the Soviet press, particularly his welcoming of progress toward the sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway. However, Soviet organs like Pravda firmly rejected Hirota's remarks concerning Soviet fortifications in the Far East and dismissed assertions of Red Army penetration into Sinkiang. Wiley notes that despite Molotov's critical speech at the VII All-Union Congress of Soviets concerning Japanese compliance with the Treaty of Portsmouth, the general tone reflects an easing of Soviet-Japanese tensions as Moscow views European developments with greater apprehension.
subfiles.title: Soviet Reaction to Hirota's Speech on Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Despatch from Ambassador Grew analyzing Foreign Minister Hirota's Diet speech and enclosing a press article by Baron Yoshiro Sakatani.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzes Foreign Minister Hirota's address to the opening of the regular Diet session, characterizing its optimistic tone as a cloak for Japan's determined policy of regional dominance in East Asia. The despatch surveys Japan's diplomatic posture toward Manchukuo, the naval disarmament talks with Britain and the United States, and the border questions with Soviet Russia. Grew encloses an article from The Japan Advertiser by Baron Yoshiro Sakatani which attributes the London naval impasse to Anglo-American policies toward China and warns against Western attempts to lead in East Asia without Japanese concurrence.
subfiles.title: Speech of the Foreign Minister, Mr. Koki Hirota, Before the Regular Session of the Diet

subfiles.about: Despatch from Ambassador Grew reporting on Diet proceedings, interpellations, and party maneuvers during the first two weeks of the 67th session.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reviews the proceedings of the 67th regular Diet from its resumption on January 22 to February 7, focusing on the Seiyukai opposition's maneuvers against the Okada Cabinet. The report discusses attacks on the government's rural relief funding, Minseito representative Takao Saito's censure of the War Ministry's November 1934 pamphlet, and interpellations regarding military spending versus diplomacy. Grew also details Seiyukai allegations that Communications Minister Tokonami accepted a 500,000 yuan payment from Marshal Chang Hsueh-liang in 1928, concluding that party government remains in desuetude with little prospect of immediate political change.
subfiles.title: Proceedings of the Imperial Diet from January 22 to February 7

subfiles.about: Despatch from the American Consulate General in Shanghai analyzing Chinese editorial reactions to Foreign Minister Hirota's Diet speech.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham transmits and reviews Chinese press commentaries on Hirota's Diet address from leading Shanghai newspapers. The independent daily Chen Pao viewed Hirota's conciliatory language toward Britain and America as defensive cover for an offensive diplomatic strategy against China and an attempt to enforce a unilateral Asiatic Monroe Doctrine. In contrast, Shih Shih Hsin Pao offered a more moderate critique, referencing Sun Yat-sen's Pan-Asian principles and expressing willingness to cooperate with Japan provided Chinese sovereignty and territorial integrity are strictly respected.
subfiles.title: Chinese Press Comments on Speech by Japanese Foreign Minister, Mr. K. Hirota

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 1161 summarizing Diet proceedings in late January 1935.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1161 extract: Hirota's address, Seiyukai attacks on relief funds, Minseito criticism of the War Office pamphlet, defense allocations, and Hirota's pledge that Japan will not go to war in his tenure.
subfiles.title: Proceedings of the Diet (Extract from Political Report No. 86)

subfiles.about: Despatch from Ambassador Grew reporting on legislative gridlock, reactionary violence, and the Minobe constitutional crisis in the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details proceedings in the 67th Diet between February 8 and March 21, noting that while the regular 1935-1936 budget passed, nearly all other government measures were blocked by Seiyukai obstruction. The despatch highlights Seijun Ando's speech in the House of Representatives attacking the cabinet for tolerating reactionary violence by rightist groups, as well as veteran leader Yukio Ozaki's somber speech on the collapse of public faith in political parties. Grew also reviews the brewing controversy surrounding Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's constitutional theory of the Emperor as an organ of the state, which prompted the House of Peers to pass a resolution demanding suppression of anti-national theories.
subfiles.title: Proceedings of the Imperial Diet from February 8 to March 21, 1935

subfiles.about: Despatch from Ambassador Grew on the adjournment of the 67th Diet, legislative failures, and cabinet durability.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the adjournment of the 67th Diet session on March 26, 1935, observing that the session produced virtually no legislation aside from the budget and the Special Business Profits Tax Bill. Crucial government measures, including voluntary rice control, cocoon stabilization, fertilizer industry regulation, and Peace Preservation Law revisions, failed enactment due to party obstruction and shelving by the House of Peers. The despatch notes that both legislative chambers passed resolutions censuring Dr. Minobe's constitutional doctrine, but concludes that the Okada Cabinet is unlikely to fall because it retains the backing of the military.
subfiles.title: Proceedings of the Imperial Diet from March 21 to the Close of the Session, March 26

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report analyzing the political, legislative, and economic ramifications of the 67th Diet session.
subfiles.summary: Weckerling reviews the 67th Diet's sudden end and failure of eleven government bills; Seiyukai obstruction, Peers' resistance, and military concern over rural distress hitting conscription.
subfiles.title: The 67th Diet - Results of the Sessions

subfiles.about: Telegram and division paraphrase reporting the reconvening of the Diet, Hirota's speech, and the sudden dissolution of parliament.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Diet reconvened January 21, 1936 with Hirota's address, then was dissolved by rescript before a no-confidence motion; election set for February 20.
subfiles.title: Reconvening and Dissolution of the Imperial Diet

subfiles.about: Document File Note and attached telegram from Nanking reporting the Chinese Foreign Office's refutation of Hirota's 'three principles'.
subfiles.summary: Peck transmits a Chinese Foreign Office statement denying China agreed to Japan's three principles, saying Japan never gave concrete terms; Chang Chun proposed normal negotiations.
subfiles.title: Chinese Foreign Office Statement on Hirota's Speech and the Three Principles

subfiles.about: Despatch from Ambassador Grew analyzing the political background and causes leading to the dissolution of the 68th Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the dissolution of the 68th Diet on January 21, 1936, following opening speeches by Premier Okada, Foreign Minister Hirota, and Finance Minister Takahashi. He explains that the Okada Cabinet dissolved parliament to avoid a non-confidence motion prepared by the Seiyukai condemning the government's handling of the Minobe Emperor-organ controversy and to escape persistent legislative paralysis. Assessing the forthcoming February 20 general elections, Grew anticipates that the Seiyukai will maintain or improve its parliamentary standing, while concluding that Japan's assertive nationalistic foreign policy will remain essentially unchanged.
subfiles.title: Dissolution of the Diet and the Internal Political Situation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 1648 summarizing political affairs, legislative proposals, and economic data.
subfiles.summary: This file entry comprises a State Department Document File Note referencing Despatch No. 1648 (Political Report No. 99) with an attached extract detailing internal political and economic developments in Japan in December 1935. The text covers the opening of the 68th Diet, Finance Minister Takahashi's rejection of fascism and support for party politics before the Showakai, and the appointment of Viscount Makoto Saito as Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal. It also summarizes a comprehensive slate of government bills prepared for the Diet—including automobile manufacturing control, rice price regulation, silk and fertilizer laws, and tariff adjustments on oil and aluminum—alongside foreign trade statistics showing an export surplus for 1935.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs and Course of Legislation (Extract from Political Report No. 99)
